prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realization of optical lattice clocks, in which many atoms are interrogated at once in a magic-wavelength trap

statement.case_for: I keep B009 as the whole configuration, and my first-round move from the CMB mapping stands. Having read all eight statements and the chair's questions, what persuades me is not that eight of us ranked it but that the reasons given are independent and checkable: the magic-wavelength lattice is a distinct principle (Doppler- and recoil-free interrogation of many atoms at once), several unrelated laboratories at RIKEN, JILA, PTB, NIST and SYRTE have reproduced and compared Sr, Yb and Hg clocks near 1e-18, and the instrument is already giving clues from nature in the form of millimetre-scale gravitational redshift, bounds on drifting constants and many-body physics in the lattice. That answers my own worry about incremental numbers: the prize would reward a new way of building a measuring device, not a better number on an old device. On credit, I read the roles as separable. Katori proposed the magic-wavelength lattice and made the first demonstration; Ye drove it to the accuracy and stability that made it a world-class tool, and his group's many-body work grew directly from the lattice platform, so it is not merely the broader JILA programme. The two-name credit is the cleanest on the table. The citation should put the invention and its realization first and leave the 1e-18 figure and the redefinition of the second out of the text, since the second has not yet been redefined.
statement.case_against: The weakest point is still precedent. The 2005 comb prize supplies the readout and the 2012 prize honoured ion control and ion clocks, so a reader can call this a third metrology prize in one lineage; the defence rests on the citation being exact about the lattice invention and I cannot make the overlap disappear. Second, no departure from known physics has been seen, so the case is about enabling power and demonstrated consequences, not a new law. Third, the two-name credit does leave out real contributors (Lemonde at SYRTE, Ludlow, Oates, Takamoto), and Olsson's request for a checked priority record has not been met by anything in the files. If the committee weighed discovery over instrument, my reserves would be B010 (Bloch, Greiner, Zoller, with the cost of dropping Esslinger and Cirac-type credit) and then my earlier first choice B050, whose WMAP versus Planck and Puget attribution remains unresolved.

responses.point: Eriksson holds B009 as her preferred prize but admits she ranked it sixth because it is not a new state of matter, and is less relaxed about the 2012 overlap than about 2005.
responses.response: I take the 2012 point more seriously than I did in round 1. The 2012 prize was about the control of individual quantum systems, with ion clocks as an application; the lattice clock differs in kind because its advance is to defeat the Doppler, recoil and Stark problems for an ensemble, so that statistics and accuracy come together. That is a different physical idea, not a refinement of Paul traps or cavity QED. I do not think the lack of a new phase of matter is a reason to hold it back, because the observed millimetre-scale redshift and the many-body spin physics in the lattice are results about nature. Where I agree with her is that the citation must name the lattice and not the clock family in general. As for her fallback B018, I share her doubt: the missing Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang step makes a three-name prize look like it skipped the proposal that pointed the experiment at HgTe.

responses.point: Pearce, the Chair, says the redefinition of the second is a consequence rather than part of the discovery, so the citation should not depend on it, and asks whether Ye's decisive contribution is the lattice clock itself or the wider JILA programme.
responses.response: On the first point I now agree and I retract part of my round-1 wording: I wrote that the pending redefinition makes the timing right, but I should not lean on an event that has not happened. The citation should be based on what is already demonstrated, and the redefinition can be mentioned in the press material at most. On Ye, my reading is that the strontium lattice clock at JILA is the realization in question: the evaluation of systematic shifts, the long coherence times and the comparisons that reached 1e-18 are what turned Katori's proposal into the world's most stable clock, and the spin-exchange and many-body work could not have been done without it. Hall's 2005 prize concerned the comb and does not claim this step, so I do not see it reducing Ye's share. I would still ask outside experts to confirm that reading, as I said I would as Secretary.

responses.point: Olsson asks whether the invention credit rests on Katori's proposal and first demonstration or also on Ye's accuracy and stability milestones, and wants the priority history checked before the citation credits both for the invention itself.
responses.response: This is the right question and I do not think the wording 'invention' alone survives it, which is why I now say 'invention and realization' with the lattice as the object. Katori has the proposal and early demonstration; Ye's group has the sustained accuracy and stability milestones. I accept that the files do not independently verify this chain and I rely on general knowledge of the clock literature, so I would send the specific lineage questions (Lemonde at SYRTE, Takamoto and the 2005 Sr demonstration, Ludlow and Oates) to the outside reviewers before the final ballot. I do not think those contributions make the two-name credit wrong, because a prize cannot go to four or five people here, but I want the citation to be accurate about who did what rather than sound like one person invented it alone.

responses.point: Johansson, who flags a conflict on B008 and says he would recuse or defer, remarks that no departure from known physics has been seen yet in the lattice clocks, and keeps B008 as an alternative.
responses.response: His remark about the absence of a departure from known physics is fair, and I added it to my case against. I would not treat it as disqualifying, because the committee has rewarded instruments that opened a regime, but it means the citation should avoid language implying new physics has been found. On B008, I keep Wallraff in mind as a missing experimental protagonist and I also share the timing worry with the 2025 circuit prize, so I have dropped it from my reserves in favour of B010. I would also support his recusal on B008 if it returned, given his Chalmers and WACQT connections and Kroll's overlapping role.

responses.point: Kroll ranks B009 first and asks whether the redefinition of the second and the new-physics searches count as realised or still prospective impact; he also notes his PhD year in John Hall's laboratory.
responses.response: I regard the redshift measurement at millimetre scales and the consistency tests between independent clocks as realised impact, and the redefinition and dark-matter searches as prospective. Prospective impact should not be in the citation. His year in Hall's laboratory is a loose link to the JILA environment, but Hall's prize was for the comb, and I would treat it as a disclosure and not a bar, provided the committee records it. He is also right that this configuration should not be treated as decided only because the files agree: agreement on the preferred part is not the same as having verified the priority record.

uncertainties: Whether the citation wording can separate the magic-wavelength lattice from the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes strongly enough to satisfy the members who are most worried about overlap.
Whether the roles of Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow and Oates change the case for exactly two names; I rely on general knowledge and have no outside expert report in hand.
Whether Ye's share is best described as the lattice clock realization itself or as the broader JILA programme, which the outside experts should settle.
For the reserve B010, which three of Bloch, Greiner, Esslinger and Zoller would be credited, and for B050 whether WMAP alone or WMAP with Planck and Puget is the right scope.
statement.conflict_note: No documented tie to Katori or Ye. My Princeton PhD under David Gross is relevant only to B050, which is not in my preferred configuration, and I co-author mainly with Thomas Van Riet. As Secretary I would formally record the disclosures of Kroll (a year in Hall's laboratory) and Johansson (B008) and support Johansson's recusal on B008 if it returns.
